scenes.title: Airflow DAGs, Operators & Sensors
scenes.narration: This lesson introduces the three building blocks of Apache Airflow: DAGs that define pipelines, operators that do the work, and sensors that wait for conditions.

scenes.title: The three core concepts
bullets: A DAG is the pipeline: tasks plus their order
An operator is a template for one unit of work
A sensor is a special operator that waits
scenes.narration: Airflow organizes work around three ideas. A DAG, or directed acyclic graph, is the pipeline itself, defining the set of tasks and the order between them. An operator is a reusable template for a single unit of work, such as running a Python function or a Bash command. A sensor is a special kind of operator whose only job is to wait until some external condition becomes true.

scenes.title: A simple DAG
scenes.code:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from datetime import datetime

with DAG(
    dag_id='daily_etl',
    schedule='@daily',
    start_date=datetime(2024, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
) as dag:
    extract = BashOperator(task_id='extract', bash_command='python extract.py')
    transform = BashOperator(task_id='transform', bash_command='dbt build')

    extract >> transform
scenes.narration: This defines a daily DAG using the context manager pattern. Inside it we create two tasks from BashOperator, one to extract and one to run dbt build. The bit-shift operator between them declares the dependency: extract must finish before transform starts. The schedule is set to daily, and catchup is disabled so Airflow does not try to backfill every past interval when the DAG first turns on. This tiny script is a complete, runnable pipeline.

scenes.title: Common operator families

right.heading: Sensors
points: Poke the condition on an interval

scenes.narration: Operators fall into a few families. Action operators actually do work: the PythonOperator runs a function, the BashOperator runs a command, and provider operators wrap cloud services. Sensors instead pause the pipeline until something is ready, such as a FileSensor waiting for a file to land or an ExternalTaskSensor waiting for a task in another DAG to complete. Sensors repeatedly poke their condition on an interval until it is satisfied.

scenes.title: How tasks flow
steps: Downstream tasks unlock as upstream succeed
scenes.narration: At runtime the Airflow scheduler continuously looks for tasks whose upstream dependencies are satisfied and queues them. An executor then runs those tasks on workers. As each upstream task succeeds, its downstream tasks become eligible and are scheduled in turn, so the whole DAG progresses automatically according to the dependencies you declared.

scenes.text: Keep DAG files lightweight and prefer reschedule-mode sensors, so waiting tasks free up worker slots instead of blocking them.
scenes.narration: A key best practice is to keep DAG files lightweight since they are parsed frequently, and to use reschedule-mode sensors so that a waiting task releases its worker slot rather than blocking it, which keeps your cluster from clogging up with idle waiters.
